rationale: LiquidFeedback's liquid democracy model was adopted by the Pirate Party Germany for binding resolutions, and the dossier shows deployment in Georgia and Myanmar -- two of the backsliding contexts I care most about. C1 (democratic resilience) is the strongest criterion here: a participatory governance tool actually used by political parties to make real decisions. The M1 backsliding-context boost (+12) elevates it further. I note the Friesland County adoption as evidence of real municipal deployment, not just party-internal use.

Open Supply Hub maps global supply chains with documented presence in Bangladesh, China, India, Brazil, and Turkey. Supply chain transparency is not my core focus, but the anti-corruption and worker-rights dimensions connect to C1, and the non-Western deployment geography (C2) is strong. The M1 boost (+12) applies for Turkey. What pushes it to the top is the combination: open-source, foundation-governed, deployed in contested contexts, with named advocacy organisations as users.

Open Contracting Partnership targets USD 2 trillion in annual public procurement -- a concrete theory of change (C4). Deployed in Ukraine, Brazil, Mexico, and across Africa and Asia. The dossier cites Brazil's medicine procurement system saving USD 75 billion as a policy outcome, which is the most specific evidence of impact in my entire ranking. M1 boost for Ukraine deployment. I discount slightly for the MEDIUM popularity risk -- OCP is well-documented and some of my scoring confidence may reflect that.

Guardian Project provides secure communications tools to journalists, activists, and human rights defenders in Egypt, Turkey, Russia, Iran, Syria, Myanmar, Belarus, and Venezuela -- the most comprehensive list of authoritarian deployments in my dataset. Every one of those countries is Freedom House 'Partly Free' or 'Not Free.' C1 and C2 both score near maximum. The M1 boost (+12) is clearly earned. I flag moderate popularity risk -- Guardian Project is well-known in digital security circles.

HOT has mapped crisis-affected areas across Afghanistan, Bangladesh, DRC, Ethiopia, and 20+ other countries. The humanitarian framing (C7) is stronger here than almost anywhere else in the list. C2 (non-Western context) scores maximum. What limits it slightly: the connection to democratic resilience (C1) is indirect -- mapping is infrastructure, not a direct power-shifting tool. Still, in crisis contexts, maps are power. M1 boost for Myanmar and Philippines deployments.

HURIDOCS equips human rights defenders with tools to mobilise information for justice and accountability -- deployed in Ukraine, Turkey, and Mexico, all countries with documented threats to civic space. This maps directly to my C1 (democratic resilience) and C2 (non-Western context). The grassroots organiser tool classification earns an M6 boost. I appreciate the specificity: the tagline names justice and accountability as goals, not vague 'awareness.' Some confidence may reflect moderate documentation richness.

Martus is a secure information collection tool for human rights activists, deployed in Afghanistan, Belarus, Burma, Colombia, and over 20 other countries. The dossier describes environments where 'capturing evidence and conveying it outside their borders may be a person's only recourse.' That framing hits C1, C2, and C7 simultaneously. Open-source with grassroots deployment capability (M6 boost). One of the few projects where the stated mission, the deployment geography, and the beneficiary population all align perfectly with my constitution.

Your Priorities has been running since 2008 -- an idea generation and deliberation platform for governments, deployed in Iceland, Portugal, Bulgaria, Serbia, and Thailand. Thailand triggers M1 (backsliding context). The deliberation focus gives it modest C3 (psychological depth) credit, rare in my ranking. C4 is supported by documented government adoption, not just theoretical impact claims.

CiviCRM is open-source constituent relationship management used by nonprofits, NGOs, and advocacy organisations worldwide, deployed in India, South Africa, and Brazil. The criteria score (76.8) is driven primarily by strong C4 (strategic clarity) and C5 (implementation maturity) -- this is a well-established tool with a decade-plus track record. I have to acknowledge that CiviCRM is one of the most thoroughly documented projects on this list, and my confidence is partly a product of that. Strip the documentation advantage and I would estimate 8-12 points lower.

VFRAME uses computer vision to detect illegal munitions and document war crimes, deployed in Syria and Ukraine. The dossier says human rights researchers rely on videos shared online to document war crimes -- and VFRAME automates the identification of cluster munitions and other prohibited weapons. This is strategic leverage (M3 potential) in service of accountability. C1, C2, and C7 all score well. The M1 backsliding-context boost applies for both Syria and Ukraine.

Open Data Editor serves nonprofits, data journalists, and activists across Cambodia, South Africa, and Ghana. The non-Western deployment geography (C2) is excellent -- these are exactly the contexts my constitution prioritises. Open-source and OKFN-backed. The criteria score (73.9) is among the highest in the dataset, driven by strong C2 and C4. What holds it back from the top: the connection to democratic resilience (C1) is through data infrastructure rather than direct power-shifting.

OpenCRVS builds civil registration systems for people who lack birth certificates -- deployed in Bangladesh, Zambia, Senegal, Kenya, Ghana, Mozambique, and Sierra Leone. The tagline says 'every person on the planet is recognised, protected and provided for from birth.' C2 scores maximum. C7 (humanitarian framing) is strong. What prevents a higher rank: the project is infrastructure for government service delivery, not directly a democratic resilience tool (C1 is moderate). Still, legal identity is precondition for civic participation.

Open Letter is a platform for creating and signing open letters for civic change, deployed in Belgium, Canada, UK, France, and the Netherlands. The Turkey deployment (listed in extended data) triggers M1. The grassroots mobilisation model earns M6 (+3). A petitioning tool maps to C1 through collective action. What limits it: predominantly Western deployment geography and no evidence of psychological sophistication (C3 near zero).

OpenProcurement is an open-source e-procurement toolkit deployed in Ukraine and Moldova -- two countries where public procurement corruption is a documented threat to democratic governance. This directly maps to C1 (democratic resilience) and M1 (backsliding context). The theory of change is unusually specific: transparent procurement reduces corruption, which reduces authoritarian capture of public resources. C4 scores well for that reason.

Ushahidi was born from Kenyan election crisis mapping and has since deployed across Kenya, Uganda, South Sudan, Nigeria, Mexico, India, and the Philippines. The Uchaguzi Platform for election monitoring directly triggers C1. 200,000+ deployments and 25 million people reached -- strong C5 (implementation maturity). I flag HIGH popularity risk: Ushahidi is one of the canonical civic tech projects, and my scoring confidence partly reflects how well-documented it is.

Polis uses AI-powered opinion clustering for large-scale deliberation, most famously in Taiwan's vTaiwan process. The psychological and behavioural dimension (C3) is stronger here than in most projects -- Polis explicitly models group opinion dynamics to find consensus. Open-source, which helps C6. I flag HIGH popularity risk -- Polis is very well-known in deliberative democracy circles, and some of my confidence reflects that. Predominantly Western/Taiwanese deployment limits C2.

Open Ownership drives transparency in corporate ownership across Zambia, Senegal, Philippines, and multiple other countries. The anti-corruption dimension directly maps to C1 and C4. Beneficial ownership transparency is a prerequisite for sanctions enforcement and anti-kleptocracy work -- close to my M3 (strategic leverage) trigger. C2 scores well for the non-Western geography. Some confidence may reflect moderate documentation richness.

Participedia is a global crowdsourcing platform cataloguing participatory processes with 1,800+ cases and 700+ methods. It serves researchers, practitioners, and policymakers. The database approach means it is infrastructure for the field rather than a direct intervention. C4 (strategic clarity) is moderate -- the impact pathway runs through knowledge diffusion, not direct deployment. Deployed primarily in Western academic contexts, which limits C2.

OPORA is the leading election monitoring network in Ukraine -- currently operating during an active war while monitoring parliamentary and presidential elections. This is the clearest possible case for C1 (democratic resilience) in my entire ranking. Deployed exclusively in Ukraine (M1 backsliding boost applies), with direct engagement with the Central Election Commission. The M2 penalty does not apply because Ukraine is not a Western democracy. The Electoral Integrity Academy shows long-term institution building, not just crisis response.

Fundacion Ciudadania Inteligente fights for democratic transformation across Latin America -- Chile, Argentina, Brazil, Colombia, Mexico. The Tu Decides campaign for the Chile 2025 elections triggers C1 directly. This is a grassroots organiser tool (M6 boost). C2 scores well for consistent non-Western deployment. The combination of election work, civic technology, and Latin American focus is rare in this dataset.

CONSUL Democracy is the participatory governance platform behind Decide Madrid, used by over 100 institutions in 35 countries. This is one of the most widely adopted participatory democracy tools globally. C1 and C5 both score well. However, the main deployments are in consolidated democracies (Spain, France), which limits C2. I flag moderate popularity risk -- CONSUL is well-known in civic tech and my confidence partly reflects documentation richness.

Tech Coops List is a curated directory of worker-owned technology cooperatives. The dossier shows deployment in the USA, Canada, Germany, Nicaragua, and Georgia. Georgia triggers M1 (backsliding context). The cooperative model is inherently anti-capture (C6). An unusual project to rank this high, but the deployment geography and grassroots economic model push it above expectations.

Creative Commons provides the licensing infrastructure underlying much of open civic technology. C6 (open access) scores maximum. The M1 boost applies because the licensing framework is used in backsliding contexts. I flag HIGH popularity risk -- Creative Commons is among the most well-known projects on this list, and strip out the documentation advantage, I would score this 8-12 points lower. The democratic resilience connection (C1) is indirect.

The Commons Social Change Library offers 1,500+ free educational resources for activists and campaigners. The Iran deployment (among Australia and US) triggers M1. The grassroots organiser classification earns M6. As a resource library rather than a tool, the C5 (implementation maturity) score reflects a different kind of deployment. I value that it explicitly serves social change advocates, not just civic tech professionals.

Bellingcat's Online Investigation Toolkit enables OSINT for investigative journalism and accountability. The strategic leverage (M3: +5) reflects that OSINT tools create material consequences for authoritarian actors -- investigations have led to sanctions, prosecutions, and international accountability. C1 scores well. The toolkit model (curated resources rather than a platform) limits C5 somewhat. Moderate popularity risk acknowledged.

Constitute Project houses the world's constitutions in a searchable database, deployed in Chile, Algeria, The Gambia, and Colombia -- all countries that have undergone constitutional processes. C1 is the primary driver: constitutional design directly shapes democratic institutions. C2 benefits from the non-Western deployment contexts. No modifiers apply. A clean, criteria-driven score.

CommunityRule helps groups define their own governance structures -- a meta-tool for democratic self-organisation. C6 (open access and anti-capture) is strong because the tool itself enables community governance. The grassroots deployment model earns M6. What limits it: no specific non-Western deployment evidence (C2 moderate), and the theory of change (C4) is diffuse.

rationale: Teaching Public Service in the Digital Age provides open-access training deployed in India, Germany, Brazil, Turkey, and Spain. Turkey triggers M1 (backsliding context). The project builds capacity within government, which connects to C1 through institutional strengthening rather than adversarial accountability. C2 benefits from the India, Brazil, and Turkey deployments.

Aleph is OCCRP's global archive for investigative journalism -- the tool behind the Panama Papers and Pandora Papers investigations. The policy outcomes are among the strongest in my dataset: a Prime Minister resigned, regulatory responses across multiple countries. M3 (strategic leverage: +6) applies because investigations create material consequences. The USAID funding dependency (50% of OCCRP budget) is a documented concern. Moderate popularity risk flagged.

Citizen OS is a free, open-source participation platform from Estonia designed for discussions and democratic decision-making. C1 (democratic resilience) is the primary criterion driver. C6 scores well -- fully open-source and community-governed. What limits it: deployed primarily in Estonia, a consolidated democracy (C2 moderate). The deliberative design gives modest C3 credit.

Diia is Ukraine's digital government ecosystem -- 20 million users accessing government services through a mobile app during wartime. This earns the M1 backsliding-context boost for documented deployment in an active conflict zone. C1 (democratic resilience) is complex here: Diia strengthens state capacity in a democracy under military attack, which is different from the usual adversarial framing. C5 (implementation maturity) is high -- this is one of the most widely adopted e-government platforms globally.

OA.Works makes academic research openly accessible, removing paywalls that disproportionately affect researchers in non-Western institutions. The open access mission maps to C6 (anti-capture) and the equity dimension maps loosely to C2. No modifiers apply. A clean criteria score driven by the open knowledge infrastructure value.

OpenSanctions integrates data from 330 sources to track sanctioned individuals and politically exposed persons. The strategic leverage dimension (M3: +6) is the key modifier -- this tool creates material consequences for authoritarian actors by enabling sanctions enforcement. The CEPA article in my evidence file specifically calls for targeted judicial sanctions; OpenSanctions is the data infrastructure that makes enforcement possible. Moderate popularity risk acknowledged.

Coral earns an M1 backsliding-context boost for deployment in Hungary, which is a signal I weight heavily. Documented policy outcome: "Adoption by major news organizations improving comment moderation prac."

Matrix is deployed in Portugal, Poland and Czech Republic, giving it strong C2 (non-Western context) scoring. Documented policy outcome: "DINUM (French government digital agency) adopted Matrix as the basis f." Moderate popularity risk -- some confidence may reflect documentation richness.

ODK (Open Data Kit) provides open-source data collection tools adopted by government health agencies for disease surveillance. Deployed internationally with strong implementation maturity (C5). The non-Western deployment geography helps C2, but the connection to democratic resilience (C1) is indirect -- data collection infrastructure, not a power-shifting tool.

Cybersecurity for Democracy's research on transparency mechanisms informed EU Digital Services Act legislation -- a documented policy outcome that boosts C4 (strategic clarity). The focus on election security and platform accountability connects to C1. What limits it: primarily US-based institutional research, limiting C2 (non-Western context).

Barcelona's adoption provides the clearest deployment evidence. I flag HIGH popularity risk -- Decidim is one of the canonical civic tech platforms, and strip the documentation advantage, I would estimate 8-12 points lower. Predominantly European deployment limits C2.

C1 (democratic resilience) is strong through the FOI pathway. Moderate popularity risk. What limits it: the criteria score could be higher with more documented non-Western deployment.
oTree is deployed in China and India, giving it strong C2 (non-Western context) scoring. Named beneficiaries: researchers, academics and economists.

The community governance and open-source credentials are strong (C6), and the M6 grassroots boost applies. What limits it: Discourse is general-purpose infrastructure, not specifically aimed at democratic resilience.

This is one of the clearest examples of deliberative democracy technology influencing real policy (C4 high). Fully open-source (C6 strong). What limits it: the deployment is primarily Taiwanese, and while Taiwan faces geopolitical pressure, the domestic democratic context is stable.

Moderate popularity risk flagged.
